name: pinneapple_perception

children.name: pinneapple_perception.audio_modal
children.doc:
Extract dominant vibration/acoustic frequencies from an audio
recording (e.g. a struck beam, plate, or shell's impulse response) via
FFT peak-picking with sub-bin parabolic frequency refinement. Depends
only on numpy/scipy (already core PINNeAPPle dependencies).

The extracted natural frequencies are directly usable to calibrate or
validate a structural-dynamics preset (e.g. comparing against a beam's
predicted modal frequencies, or as a `DataConstraint` target for an
inverse-problem fit of an unknown material/geometry parameter that the
preset's frequency depends on).

functions.name: extract_dominant_frequencies
functions.sig: (waveform: np.ndarray, sample_rate: float, n_peaks: int = 5, min_freq: float = 0.0, max_freq: Optional[float] = None, window: str = 'hann') -> List[Tuple[float, float]]
functions.doc:
Return the `n_peaks` most prominent frequency components of
`waveform`, as a list of (frequency_Hz, amplitude) tuples sorted by
descending amplitude.

Parameters
----------
waveform : 1D array, a single-channel audio/vibration time series.
sample_rate : samples per second (Hz).
n_peaks : how many dominant frequencies to return.
min_freq, max_freq : restrict the search to this frequency band (e.g.
    to exclude DC/very-low-frequency drift, or to focus on a known
    expected mode range). `max_freq` defaults to the Nyquist frequency.
window : window function applied before the FFT to reduce spectral
    leakage ("hann" or "none").

children.summary: Extract dominant vibration/acoustic frequencies from an audio recording (e.g. a struck beam, plate, or shell's impulse response) via FFT peak-picking with sub-bin parabolic frequency refinement.

children.name: pinneapple_perception.change_detection
children.doc:
Change detection between two multispectral images of the same place: per-band mean absolute reflectance change
and NDVI change against thresholds, a comparison figure and a self-contained HTML report.

Inputs are plain arrays (H, W, 3) in band order red, green, blue (Sentinel-2 B4, B3, B2) and, for NDVI, a real
near-infrared band (H, W) (B8): no NIR is ever synthesised. Sentinel-2 surface reflectance is stored as
DN = 10000 x reflectance, so the default ``reflectance_scale`` is 10000; 3000 is only the display stretch of the
RGB previews. :mod:`pinneapple_perception.sentinel2` fetches such images from Google Earth Engine.

Moved here from the PINNeAPPle-apps ``satellite_change_monitoring`` product (OrbitWatch), which extracted it from
a notebook with two fixes kept here:

1. **The notebook's NDVI was fake.** Its own comment says so:
   "Simulando que banda NIR é R + 400 (ajuste conforme sua fonte real)"
   -- i.e. it approximated the near-infrared band as
   ``nir = red_band + 400``, a made-up placeholder, rather than fetching
   Sentinel-2's real NIR band (B8). `compute_ndvi` here takes a REAL nir
   array as an explicit required argument -- `pinneapple_perception.sentinel2`
   fetches the real B8 band alongside B4/B3/B2 for exactly this reason.
   There is no fallback path in this module that fabricates an NIR band;
   a caller without a real NIR array should not call `compute_ndvi` at
   all (the app layer makes this optional per-request, not a silent
   default).
2. **The notebook conflated a display-stretch constant with a physical
   reflectance-change threshold.** It divided differences by 3000 for
   BOTH the RGB visualization stretch (`img / 3000`, a common contrast
   trick for Sentinel-2's 0-10000 raw digital-number range) AND the
   quantitative band-change threshold check (`mean_diff / 3000 > 0.05`).
   Real Sentinel-2 Surface Reflectance products scale reflectance as
   raw_DN / 10000 (documented by ESA/Copernicus), so a diff normalized by
   3000 is not actually "5% of true reflectance change" -- it's roughly
   3.3x more sensitive than that. This module defaults
   `reflectance_scale=10000.0` (the real, physically correct SR scale)
   for the quantitative threshold, and keeps 3000 available separately,
   only for the RGB preview's own contrast stretch (`rgb_preview_stretch`
   below), where it is purely a display choice with no claim to physical
   meaning. Pass `reflectance_scale=3000.0` to reproduce the original
   notebook's (physically-inconsistent) threshold behavior exactly.

functions.name: band_difference
functions.sig: (img_a: np.ndarray, img_b: np.ndarray, band_index: int, band_name: str, threshold: float = DEFAULT_BAND_DIFF_THRESHOLD, reflectance_scale: float = DEFAULT_REFLECTANCE_SCALE) -> BandChangeResult
functions.doc:
Real per-band mean-absolute-difference change check, same
computation as the original notebook's `detecta_mudanca` (mean of
|img_b - img_a| for one band, normalized, compared to a threshold),
but with an explicit, physically-meaningful `reflectance_scale`
(default the real Sentinel-2 SR scale, 10000) instead of the
original's conflated 3000 display-stretch constant -- see this
module's docstring.

functions.name: compute_ndvi
functions.sig: (red: np.ndarray, nir: np.ndarray, eps: float = 1e-06) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Real NDVI: (NIR - RED) / (NIR + RED + eps). `red` and `nir` must
both be REAL band arrays (Sentinel-2 B4 and B8 respectively) -- this
function has no fallback that fabricates either band. Same formula
as the original notebook's `calcula_ndvi`, applied to a real NIR
input instead of the original's `red + 400` placeholder.

functions.name: ndvi_change
functions.sig: (ndvi_a: np.ndarray, ndvi_b: np.ndarray, threshold: float = DEFAULT_NDVI_THRESHOLD) -> NdviChangeResult

functions.name: analyze_pair
functions.sig: (rgb_a: np.ndarray, rgb_b: np.ndarray, date_a: str, date_b: str, nir_a: np.ndarray | None = None, nir_b: np.ndarray | None = None, band_diff_threshold: float = DEFAULT_BAND_DIFF_THRESHOLD, ndvi_threshold: float = DEFAULT_NDVI_THRESHOLD, reflectance_scale: float = DEFAULT_REFLECTANCE_SCALE) -> PairAnalysis
functions.doc:
Real per-pair change analysis: three band-difference checks
(red/green/blue) always run; NDVI is computed and checked only if
real `nir_a`/`nir_b` arrays are supplied (never fabricated).
`date_a` should chronologically precede `date_b` -- the caller is
responsible for ordering (this fixes a real, if cosmetic,
inconsistency in the original notebook: its narrative text in cell 7
labeled pairs as "between dates[i+1] and dates[i]" while its HTML
report in cell 8 labeled the SAME pairs "dates[i] -> dates[i+1]",
reversed direction for an otherwise-identical diff computation).

functions.name: rgb_preview_stretch
functions.doc:
Purely a display contrast stretch (clip to [0,1] after dividing by
a fixed constant) -- matches the original notebook's `img/3000`
preview trick. This has NO physical-reflectance meaning (see this
module's docstring); it is only ever used for the RGB preview panels,
never for the quantitative threshold checks.

functions.name: render_comparison_figure
functions.sig: (rgb_a: np.ndarray, rgb_b: np.ndarray, date_a: str, date_b: str, ndvi_a: np.ndarray | None = None, ndvi_b: np.ndarray | None = None) -> bytes
functions.doc:
Render the same-style comparison grid the original notebook
produced (RGB pair + diff, per-band diff maps, and -- when real NDVI
arrays are supplied -- an NDVI before/after/delta row), as real PNG
bytes (matplotlib `Agg` backend, no display needed).

functions.name: render_html_report
functions.sig: (pairs: list, images_png: list, lon: float, lat: float, buffer_m: float, has_ndvi: bool) -> str

children.summary: Change detection between two multispectral images of the same place: per-band mean absolute reflectance change and NDVI change against thresholds, a comparison figure and a self-contained HTML report.

children.name: pinneapple_perception.image_geometry
children.doc:
Extract boundary/geometry point clouds from an image -- e.g. a photo
or scan of a physical part's cross-section -- for use as a domain
boundary in `pinneapple_design.geometry` or as boundary-condition
selector data. Depends only on numpy/scipy (already core PINNeAPPle
dependencies).

Method: binarize the image (threshold), then extract the boundary as the
set of foreground pixels adjacent to a background pixel (a standard
morphological boundary: `foreground AND NOT erode(foreground)`), and
order them into a single closed contour by nearest-neighbor walking
(sufficient for simple, single-blob shapes; a genuinely disconnected or
highly concave/branching shape may need per-component ordering -- see
`extract_boundary_points`'s `ordered` parameter).

functions.name: extract_boundary_points
functions.sig: (image: np.ndarray, threshold: Optional[float] = None, units_per_pixel: float = 1.0, ordered: bool = True) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Extract the boundary of the foreground region(s) in `image` as a
point cloud.

Parameters
----------
image : (H, W) grayscale array (float or int). RGB images should be
    converted to grayscale first (e.g. `image.mean(axis=-1)`).
threshold : foreground/background cutoff. Defaults to the image's own
    mean value (Otsu-lite; good enough for a roughly bimodal image --
    pass an explicit value for anything else).
units_per_pixel : physical length per pixel, applied to the returned
    coordinates.
ordered : if True (default), order the boundary points into a single
    connected walk (nearest-neighbor greedy ordering) so the result
    can be used directly as a polygon/contour. If False, returns the
    unordered set of boundary pixel coordinates (faster, and correct
    for multi-component shapes where "ordered" doesn't make sense).

Returns
-------
(N, 2) float32 array of (x, y) boundary point coordinates, in
physical units (image row/column, i.e. y increases downward, matching
standard image-array convention -- flip the y column if a
y-increases-upward convention is needed downstream).

functions.name: estimate_bounding_circle
functions.doc:
Least-squares circle fit (algebraic Kasa method) to a boundary
point cloud -- a quick, standard way to validate/characterize a
roughly-circular extracted boundary (e.g. a pipe or shaft
cross-section). Returns (center_x, center_y, radius).

children.summary: Extract boundary/geometry point clouds from an image -- e.g. a photo or scan of a physical part's cross-section -- for use as a domain boundary in pinneapple_design.geometry or as boundary-condition ...

children.name: pinneapple_perception.piv_tools
children.doc:
Around :mod:`.video_piv`: reading frames from a video or image files, the vector-grid size a setting gives, a
summary of a PIV result, and window / search-margin advice from the expected displacement.

* :func:`decode_video` -- a video file to a (T, H, W) float grayscale array through ``ffprobe`` / ``ffmpeg``
  subprocesses (``FFmpegMissing`` when they are not on PATH).
* :func:`decode_image_frames` -- image files (PNG, JPEG, ...; Pillow) to (T, H, W), in file-name order.
* :func:`piv_grid_count` -- vectors per frame pair, with the same loop bounds as ``piv_velocity_field``: a window
  is used only when its whole search region fits in the image (half window + search margin from every border).
* :func:`summarize_piv` -- vector count, the windows withheld for border safety (against a grid that only needs
  room for the window), mean / max speed. ``piv_velocity_field`` has no correlation-quality (signal-to-noise)
  rejection; the only vectors it drops are those border windows.
* :func:`piv_parameter_guide` -- the one-quarter rule (Raffel, Willert, Wereley & Kompenhans, *Particle Image
  Velocimetry: A Practical Guide*, 3rd ed., Springer 2018): keep the particle displacement below about a quarter
  of the interrogation window, a search margin of 1.5 x the displacement, 50 % overlap.

Moved here from the PINNeAPPle-apps ``piv_analysis_api`` product (FlowTrace).

functions.name: decode_video
functions.doc: (T, H, W) float64 grayscale frames of the video at ``path`` (ffprobe for the size, ffmpeg for the pixels).

functions.name: decode_image_frames
functions.doc: (T, H, W) grayscale frames from ``(file name, bytes)`` pairs, sorted by file name (use zero-padded names).

functions.name: piv_grid_count
functions.sig: (height: int, width: int, window_size: int, search_margin: int, step: int | None = None, *, margin: int | None = None) -> tuple[int, int]
functions.doc: (rows, cols) of interrogation windows ``piv_velocity_field`` uses on an H x W frame.

functions.name: summarize_piv
functions.sig: (seq: dict, frame_shape: tuple, window_size: int, search_margin: int, step: int | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc: Counts and speeds of a ``piv_velocity_sequence`` result on frames of shape (T, H, W).

functions.name: piv_parameter_guide
functions.sig: (displacement_px: float, width_px: int, height_px: int) -> dict
functions.doc: Window size, search margin and step for an expected displacement (px per frame), with warnings.

children.summary: Around .video_piv: reading frames from a video or image files, the vector-grid size a setting gives, a summary of a PIV result, and window / search-margin advice from the expected displacement.

children.name: pinneapple_perception.sentinel2
children.doc:
Sentinel-2 surface-reflectance images of a point from Google Earth Engine, as arrays for
:mod:`pinneapple_perception.change_detection` (bands B4, B3, B2 and the real NIR band B8).

Credentials come from the environment only, never from code or files in this repository:

* ``EE_PROJECT_ID`` -- the Google Cloud project registered for Earth Engine (https://code.earthengine.google.com/register,
  with the Earth Engine API enabled in that project);
* either ``EE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL`` + ``EE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY_FILE`` (path to the service account's JSON key,
  kept outside the repository and the image) for a server, or a one-time ``earthengine authenticate`` on the host,
  which stores a refresh token under ``~/.config/earthengine/``.

Without them :func:`ee_initialize` raises :class:`EarthEngineUnavailable` with these steps: no imagery is
fabricated. Needs the optional ``earthengine-api`` and ``geemap`` packages.

Moved here from the PINNeAPPle-apps ``satellite_change_monitoring`` product (OrbitWatch), extracted from a notebook;
images are returned oldest first (the notebook fetched newest first and labelled pairs in both directions).

classes.name: EarthEngineUnavailable
classes.doc:
Raised when ee.Initialize() genuinely fails -- no credential, no
project, or the Earth Engine API not enabled for the given project.
Carries the real underlying exception's message plus the concrete
remediation steps from this module's docstring, so a caller sees
exactly what a real deployment needs rather than a bare stack trace.

functions.name: ee_initialize
functions.doc:
Real ee.Initialize() call. Tries a service account credential if
EE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL + EE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY_FILE are set (the
real, non-interactive path for a server deployment); otherwise falls
through to ee's default persistent-credential lookup (populated by a
prior real `earthengine authenticate` run). Never silently succeeds
with fabricated access -- either a real `ee.Initialize()` call
genuinely succeeds, or this raises `EarthEngineUnavailable` with a
concrete remediation message.

functions.name: fetch_sentinel2_sequence
functions.sig: (lon: float, lat: float, buffer_m: float = 5000.0, start_date: str = '2024-01-01', end_date: str = '2025-07-27', max_cloud_pct: float = 10.0, n_images: int = 5, scale: int = 10, project: str | None = None) -> list
functions.doc:
Real fetch of the n_images most recent, least-cloudy Sentinel-2 SR
images intersecting a buffered point, returned oldest-to-newest
(chronological order -- the original notebook fetched newest-first
and then had two of its own cells label "before/after" in opposite
directions for the same pairs; sorting chronologically here avoids
reproducing that ambiguity). Same collection/filter/band logic as
the source notebook, with one real fix: this also fetches the real
NIR band (B8) alongside B4/B3/B2, instead of that notebook's fake
`nir = red + 400` placeholder -- see change_detection's module docstring.

Raises EarthEngineUnavailable if ee.Initialize() fails (see above).
Raises ValueError if fewer than 2 images are found for the given
region/date range/cloud filter -- the same real "need >= 2 images"
check the notebook made explicit in its own cell 6.

children.summary: Sentinel-2 surface-reflectance images of a point from Google Earth Engine, as arrays for pinneapple_perception.change_detection (bands B4, B3, B2 and the real NIR band B8).

children.name: pinneapple_perception.video_piv
children.doc:
Extract a velocity field from a video (image pair/sequence) using
cross-correlation Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) -- the actual
standard technique experimental fluid dynamicists use to turn a video of
a seeded/textured flow into a velocity field, not a generic computer-
vision optical-flow method repurposed for this. Depends only on
numpy/scipy (both already core PINNeAPPle dependencies) -- no new
third-party dependency needed.

Algorithm (per pair of consecutive frames):
  1. Divide the first frame into square interrogation windows on a grid
     (with optional overlap).
  2. For each window, cross-correlate it (FFT-based, normalized) against
     the corresponding region of the second frame.
  3. The correlation peak location gives the most likely pixel
     displacement for that window; a 3-point parabolic fit around the
     peak in each axis gives sub-pixel accuracy (the standard PIV
     sub-pixel refinement, e.g. Raffel et al., "Particle Image
     Velocimetry: A Practical Guide").
  4. Displacement -> velocity via the frame interval `dt` and an optional
     physical calibration (`units_per_pixel`).

The extracted (x, y, u, v) field is a plain numpy array bundle -- pass it
directly as `x_data`/`y_data` to `solve_pde`/`compile_problem` (e.g. as a
`DataConstraint` on a `navier_stokes_incompressible`-family preset) to
train a PINN surrogate constrained by real video-derived velocity
observations, the same way any other sparse tracking/data-constraint
this library already supports is used.

functions.name: piv_velocity_field
functions.sig: (frame_a: np.ndarray, frame_b: np.ndarray, window_size: int = 32, search_margin: int = 16, step: Optional[int] = None, dt: float = 1.0, units_per_pixel: float = 1.0) -> Dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Cross-correlation PIV velocity field between two grayscale frames.

Parameters
----------
frame_a, frame_b : (H, W) arrays, same shape (grayscale/single-channel;
    pass e.g. `frame[..., :3].mean(axis=-1)` for an RGB frame).
window_size : interrogation window side length, in pixels.
search_margin : how many pixels beyond the window the search region in
    frame_b extends on each side (bounds the maximum detectable
    displacement to +/- search_margin pixels).
step : grid spacing between window centers, in pixels (defaults to
    `window_size`, i.e. no overlap).
dt : time interval between the two frames (s) -- divides displacement
    to give velocity.
units_per_pixel : physical length per pixel (e.g. meters/pixel from a
    camera calibration) -- multiplies displacement to convert from
    pixels to physical length before dividing by dt.

Returns
-------
dict with keys "x", "y" (window-center pixel coordinates, in physical
units) and "u", "v" (velocity components, physical units per second).
All four are flattened 1D arrays of the same length (one entry per
interrogation window), directly usable as a `DataConstraint`'s
x/y data for `solve_pde`.

functions.name: piv_velocity_sequence
functions.doc:
Run `piv_velocity_field` on every consecutive pair in a video
(`frames`: (T, H, W) array) and stack the results with a `t` column,
ready for a 3D (x, y, t) `DataConstraint`.

doc:
pinneapple_perception — extract physics observations from images,
video, and audio, for use as `DataConstraint` targets or boundary
geometry anywhere else in PINNeAPPle.

This is the inverse direction of `pinneapple_worldmodel` (which renders
physics simulations INTO photorealistic synthetic images/video for
training data generation) -- here, real-world images/video/audio go IN
and physics observations (velocity fields, boundary geometry, modal
frequencies) come OUT.

Sub-modules
-----------
video_piv
    Cross-correlation Particle Image Velocimetry: extract a velocity
    field from a video of a seeded/textured flow -- the standard
    experimental-fluid-dynamics technique, not a generic optical-flow
    method repurposed for this.
image_geometry
    Extract a boundary point cloud (and, for round parts, a fitted
    circle) from an image -- e.g. a photo or scan of a part's
    cross-section -- for use as domain geometry.
audio_modal
    Extract dominant vibration/acoustic frequencies from a recording
    (e.g. an impulse-response test) via FFT peak-picking with sub-bin
    frequency refinement -- for calibrating/validating structural-
    dynamics presets against a real measured part.

All three depend only on numpy/scipy (already core PINNeAPPle
dependencies) -- no new third-party dependency required. Every technique
here was validated against a synthetic, known-ground-truth case before
being shipped (see `tests/test_perception.py`): PIV against a known
sub-pixel image shift, boundary/circle extraction against a known
circle, and modal extraction against known sine-wave frequencies.

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_perception import piv_velocity_field
>>> field = piv_velocity_field(frame_a, frame_b, dt=1/30, units_per_pixel=1e-3)
>>> # field["x"], field["y"], field["u"], field["v"] -- feed directly into
>>> # a DataConstraint on a navier_stokes_incompressible-family preset.
summary: Extract physics observations from images, video, and audio, for use as DataConstraint targets or boundary geometry anywhere else in PINNeAPPle.
